name: Spaghetti alla Carbonara
description: Roman pasta of guanciale (cured pork cheek), raw eggs or yolks, pecorino romano and black pepper; the egg and cheese are mixed with the hot pasta off the heat to make a creamy sauce. One of Rome's famous pastas alongside cacio e pepe, gricia and amatriciana, and cream is not used in most Italian recipes.
how_to_eat: Eat straight away while the sauce is still glossy.
how_to_order: Ask for 'carbonara' at any Roman trattoria.

name: Cacio e Pepe
description: Tonnarelli or spaghetti tossed with grated pecorino romano, black pepper and starchy pasta water into a creamy sauce. Said to come from the shepherds of central Italy, it is one of the famous pasta dishes of Roman cuisine.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tonnarelli cacio e pepe' at Roman trattorias.

name: Pasta all'Amatriciana
description: Pasta (usually bucatini or spaghetti) in a sauce of guanciale, tomato and pecorino, named after the town of Amatrice in Lazio. 'Amatriciana tradizionale' is registered as an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed.
how_to_order: Ask for 'bucatini all'amatriciana' at Roman trattorias.

name: Supplì
description: Fried rice croquettes of risotto rice mixed with meat sauce, Parmesan and egg, with a piece of mozzarella in the centre, coated in breadcrumbs. A classic Roman snack, first sold in friggitorie and now served in pizzerias as an antipasto.
how_to_eat: Pull it apart to see the mozzarella stretch like a telephone cord ('supplì al telefono').
how_to_order: Order one or two at a pizza al taglio shop or as a starter in a pizzeria.

name: Carciofi alla Giudia
description: Whole Romanesco artichokes deep-fried twice in olive oil until the leaves open and crisp like a flower. A signature of Roman Jewish cuisine, served in the restaurants of the Roman Ghetto in springtime.
how_to_eat: Eat the crisp outer leaves with your fingers and the tender heart with a fork.
how_to_order: Look for it in restaurants of the Jewish Ghetto in Rome.

name: Maritozzo
description: A soft sweet bun of flour, eggs, honey and butter, split open and filled generously with whipped cream. Typical of Rome, where a Maritozzo Day is held every December.
how_to_eat: Eat in the morning with a cappuccino.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'maritozzo con la panna' at a Roman bar or pasticceria.

name: Neapolitan Pizza
description: Round pizza with a soft, thin dough and high edges, baked for 60-90 seconds in a very hot wood-fired oven and traditionally topped with San Marzano tomatoes and buffalo mozzarella or fior di latte. It is registered as an EU Traditional Speciality Guaranteed and the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo is on UNESCO's list.
how_to_eat: Eat with knife and fork, or fold it 'a portafoglio' (wallet-style).
how_to_order: Order a 'margherita' or 'marinara' at a Naples pizzeria.

name: Spaghetti alle Vongole
description: Spaghetti with fresh clams cooked in olive oil with plenty of garlic and parsley, sometimes with a splash of white wine. A southern Italian coastal classic, made 'in bianco' (without tomato) or 'in rosso' with tomatoes, and a Neapolitan Christmas Eve favourite.
how_to_order: Ask for 'spaghetti alle vongole' at seafood restaurants along the coast.

name: Sfogliatella
description: Shell-shaped pastry of many thin layers of dough separated by lard, with a filling based on semolina and ricotta. The 'riccia' is the crisp layered type, the 'frolla' a softer shortcrust version; Naples pastry cook Pasquale Pintauro made it famous from 1818.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, fresh from the oven.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'sfogliatella riccia' at a Neapolitan pasticceria.

name: Babà
description: A small yeast cake of eggs, milk and butter soaked in rum syrup, sometimes filled with whipped cream or pastry cream. Invented in France, it became a popular Neapolitan speciality.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'babà' at any Neapolitan pastry shop.

name: Insalata Caprese
description: A salad of sliced fresh mozzarella, tomatoes and basil, dressed with olive oil, named after the island of Capri. Its colours echo the Italian flag.
how_to_order: Order as an antipasto or light lunch.

name: Limoncello
description: Lemon liqueur made by steeping lemon zest in spirit, then mixing it with sugar syrup. Produced mainly around the Gulf of Naples and the Amalfi Coast, it is Italy's second-most popular liqueur and is traditionally served chilled after dinner.
how_to_eat: Sip it ice-cold from a small glass after dinner.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'limoncello' as a digestivo after a meal.

name: Pizza Fritta
description: Neapolitan fried pizza: pizza dough filled (typically with ricotta, provola and cicoli pork cracklings or Neapolitan salami), folded and deep-fried. Born as a cheap 'pizza of the people' sold in the streets of post-war Naples.
how_to_eat: Eat hot from paper, standing in the street.
how_to_order: Buy it from a 'friggitoria' or pizza fritta stall in central Naples.

name: Arancini
description: Deep-fried breaded rice balls (conical in eastern Sicily, e.g. Catania and Messina) most commonly stuffed with meat ragù, cheese and peas, or with prosciutto and mozzarella. A staple of Sicilian street food, said to date from the island's 10th-century Arab period.
how_to_eat: Eat hot as a snack, by hand.
how_to_order: Ask for an 'arancina al ragù' at a rosticceria or bar.

name: Cannoli
description: Tubes of crisp fried pastry filled with sweetened sheep's-milk ricotta, with candied fruit and chocolate chips. The shells are made with lard and traditionally fried in lard; it is one of Sicily's best-known pastries.
how_to_eat: Eat right after filling so the shell stays crisp.
how_to_order: Ask for a cannolo filled to order at a pasticceria.

name: Caponata
description: A sweet-and-sour (agrodolce) dish of chopped fried aubergine and other vegetables with tomato sauce, celery, olives, capers and olive oil. One of Sicily's classic vegetable dishes, historically associated with the island's Jewish community.
how_to_eat: Eat at room temperature with bread.
how_to_order: Order as a 'contorno' or antipasto.

name: Pasta alla Norma
description: Pasta with tomato sauce, fried aubergine, basil and grated ricotta salata, from Catania. It is said to be named after Bellini's opera 'Norma'.
how_to_order: Ask for 'pasta alla Norma', especially in Catania.

name: Granita
description: A semi-frozen dessert of sugar, water and flavourings such as lemon, almond, coffee or fruit, stirred while freezing into fine ice crystals. In Messina it is creamy and traditionally eaten for breakfast with a brioche.
how_to_eat: Eat with a soft brioche col tuppo dipped into it.
how_to_order: Order 'granita con brioche' at a Sicilian bar.

name: Cassata Siciliana
description: Round cake of sponge moistened with fruit juice or liqueur, layered with sweetened ricotta and candied fruit, covered in marzipan and icing and decorated. It is believed to have originated in Palermo during the Arab period.
how_to_order: Buy a slice at a Sicilian pasticceria.

name: Tortellini in Brodo
description: Small ring-shaped egg-pasta parcels filled with pork loin, prosciutto, mortadella, Parmesan, egg and nutmeg, served in capon broth. A symbol of the cuisine of Bologna and Modena, both of which claim to be its birthplace.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tortellini in brodo' at a Bolognese trattoria.

name: Tagliatelle al Ragù
description: Fresh egg tagliatelle with Bologna's slow-cooked meat ragù of beef, pork, soffritto, wine and a little tomato. In Bologna ragù is served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti.
how_to_order: Ask for 'tagliatelle al ragù' in Bologna.

name: Lasagne alla Bolognese
description: Baked layers of green spinach egg pasta, ragù, béchamel and Parmigiano Reggiano. The Bolognese version of Italy's best-known baked pasta.
how_to_order: Ask for 'lasagne verdi' at trattorias in Bologna.

name: Piadina Romagnola
description: Thin flatbread of flour, lard or olive oil, salt and water, cooked on a griddle and filled with cheeses, cured meats or vegetables. It holds EU Protected Geographical Indication status for Romagna.
how_to_eat: Eat it folded and warm, straight from the kiosk.
how_to_order: Order at a roadside 'piadineria' kiosk in Romagna.

name: Gnocco Fritto
description: Puffy diamonds of dough fried (traditionally in lard) until hollow, served with cured meats such as prosciutto, salami and mortadella. Known as crescentina in Bologna and torta fritta in Parma.
how_to_eat: Eat hot, wrapped around a slice of cured meat.
how_to_order: Order a plate with 'salumi misti' at Emilian trattorias.

name: Zuppa Inglese
description: Layered dessert of sponge cake or savoiardi biscuits dipped in red Alchermes liqueur, alternating with custard and often chocolate custard. One account credits its creation to the court of the Este dukes of Ferrara.
how_to_order: Look for it on the dessert list of Emilian trattorias.

name: Bistecca alla Fiorentina
description: A thick T-bone steak (5-6 cm) from a young steer or heifer, traditionally of the Chianina breed, grilled and usually served rare. One of the most famous dishes of Tuscan cuisine; restaurant steaks typically weigh 0.9-1.2 kg and are priced by the kilo.
how_to_eat: Share one steak between two or more people; it is served rare.
how_to_order: Order by weight (usually about 1 kg upwards) at a Florentine trattoria.

name: Ribollita
description: A thick Tuscan bread soup of stale bread, cannellini beans, cavolo nero, cabbage and vegetables; the name means 'reboiled'. It was originally made by reboiling leftover vegetable soup with bread.
how_to_eat: Eat with a drizzle of fresh olive oil on top.
how_to_order: Ask for 'ribollita' at Tuscan trattorias in the cold months.

name: Pappa al Pomodoro
description: A thick soup of stale Tuscan bread cooked with tomatoes, garlic, basil and olive oil. Served hot, at room temperature or chilled, and by Tuscan tradition never with cheese.
how_to_order: Order as a 'primo' at Tuscan trattorias.

name: Lampredotto
description: The fourth stomach of the cow, slow-cooked in vegetable broth with herbs, chopped and served in a bread roll with green sauce or a spicy sauce. Florence's classic street food sandwich.
how_to_eat: Ask for the top half of the roll dipped in the broth ('bagnato').
how_to_order: Buy a 'panino col lampredotto' from a tripe cart in Florence.

name: Cantucci Toscani
description: Twice-baked dry almond biscuits made with flour, sugar, eggs and almonds, originating in Prato. 'Cantuccini Toscani' is registered as an EU Protected Geographical Indication.
how_to_eat: Dip them in a glass of Vin Santo dessert wine.
how_to_order: Ask for 'cantucci e vin santo' at the end of a Tuscan meal.

name: Panforte di Siena
description: Chewy, dense Christmas cake of fruit and nuts associated with Siena, dating back to at least the 13th century, when it was a honey-and-pepper bread. Panforte has held EU Protected Geographical Indication status since 2013.
how_to_eat: Eat in thin wedges, often at Christmas.
how_to_order: Buy it at bakeries and shops in Siena.

name: Ricciarelli
description: Soft, chewy almond biscuits made from almond paste, sugar and egg whites, dusted with icing sugar. 'Ricciarelli di Siena' is an EU Protected Geographical Indication.
how_to_order: Buy them at Sienese bakeries, especially around Christmas.

name: Risotto alla Milanese
description: Saffron-yellow risotto, cooked in broth and traditionally made with beef marrow; its colour gives it the nickname risotto giallo. Milan's best-known rice dish, often served with ossobuco as a one-course meal.
how_to_order: Ask for 'risotto alla milanese', or 'risotto con ossobuco', in Milan.

name: Cotoletta alla Milanese
description: Bone-in veal loin chop, breaded and fried in butter. One of Milan's most typical dishes, often compared to the Wiener schnitzel.
how_to_eat: Squeeze lemon over it and eat with a fork and knife.
how_to_order: Order at traditional Milanese restaurants.

name: Trofie al Pesto
description: Short, thin twisted Ligurian pasta, believed to come from Sori near Genoa, served with pesto genovese, a sauce of basil, pine nuts, garlic, Parmesan, pecorino and olive oil. Pesto originated in Genoa.
how_to_order: Ask for 'trofie al pesto' in Genoa and the Cinque Terre.

name: Focaccia Genovese
description: Flat oven-baked bread about a centimetre high with marked dimples, brushed before its final rise with an emulsion of olive oil, water and coarse salt. In Genoa it is eaten at any time of day, and at breakfast it is often dipped in cappuccino or milk.
how_to_eat: Locals dip it in their morning cappuccino.
how_to_order: Buy a slice by weight at any Genoese bakery (panificio).

name: Tiramisù
description: Spoon dessert of savoiardi biscuits dipped in coffee, layered with a cream of mascarpone, egg yolks and sugar and dusted with cocoa. It originated in north-eastern Italy, and a widely reported account credits its invention to a Treviso restaurant in 1969.
how_to_order: Order as a dessert in any restaurant.

name: Spritz
description: Aperitif of prosecco, a bitter liqueur such as Aperol, Campari or, in Venice, Select, and soda water, served with ice. It began under Habsburg rule in the Veneto, when wine was diluted with water, and the original spritz veneziano was created in Venice in 1920.
how_to_eat: Drink at aperitivo time with cicchetti (small bar snacks).
how_to_order: Ask for 'uno spritz' and say Aperol or Campari.

name: Vitello Tonnato
description: Cold sliced poached veal covered with a creamy sauce of tuna, anchovies, capers and mayonnaise. A Piedmontese antipasto, popular in summer.
how_to_order: Order as an antipasto in Piedmontese restaurants.

name: Orecchiette con Cime di Rapa
local_name: Orecchiette con le cime di rapa
description: Small ear-shaped durum wheat pasta served with turnip tops, often dressed with garlic, anchovies, chilli and olive oil and finished with cacioricotta cheese. It is the most iconic Apulian pasta dish, and women still make orecchiette by hand in Bari's old town.
how_to_order: Ask for 'orecchiette con cime di rapa' in Bari.

name: Focaccia Barese
description: Soft focaccia from Apulia made with re-milled durum wheat semolina and boiled potato in the dough, classically topped with fresh tomatoes and/or olives. Sold in bakeries across Bari and the surrounding provinces.
how_to_order: Buy a slice at a bakery in Bari.

name: Panzerotti
description: Half-moon turnovers of dough filled with tomato and mozzarella, then deep-fried. A popular Apulian street food.
how_to_eat: Eat hot but carefully, the filling is very hot.
how_to_order: Buy at friggitorie and bakeries in Bari.

name: Pasticciotto
description: Shortcrust pastry (traditionally made with lard) filled with custard and baked. The typical breakfast pastry of Lecce, which named it the city's typical cake.
how_to_eat: Eat warm for breakfast with a coffee.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'pasticciotto' at a bar in Lecce.

name: Taralli
description: Crunchy ring-shaped crackers of flour, olive oil, white wine and salt, classically flavoured with fennel seeds. A popular Apulian snack, eaten as is or dunked in wine.
how_to_eat: Eat as a snack with a glass of wine.
how_to_order: Buy packets at bakeries and grocery shops.

name: Culurgiones
description: Pasta dumplings closed with an ear-of-wheat pleat, filled with potato, pecorino, mint and garlic, and dressed with olive oil or, more recently, tomato sauce and pecorino. 'Culurgionis d'Ogliastra' has been an EU Protected Geographical Indication since 2015.
how_to_order: Look for 'culurgiones' on menus in eastern Sardinia.

name: Porceddu
description: Suckling pig of no more than 6-7 kg roasted on a spit, salted halfway through so the skin turns crisp, and flavoured with herbs such as myrtle, thyme and mint. One of Sardinia's most famous dishes, once eaten by shepherds at Easter.
how_to_order: Order at agriturismi and traditional restaurants; it is often pre-ordered.

name: Pane Carasau
description: Very thin, crisp Sardinian flatbread of durum wheat baked twice; Italians call it 'carta da musica' (sheet music) because of its thinness. It was made for shepherds away from home for months, as it keeps up to a year.
how_to_eat: Eat as is, or as 'pane guttiau' drizzled with olive oil and salt.
how_to_order: Served free on the table in Sardinian restaurants; sold in packs in shops.

name: Seada
description: Large fried semolina-and-lard pastry discs filled with soured pecorino and lemon peel, served covered with honey. A typical fried sweet of Sardinian tradition.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with plenty of honey.
how_to_order: Order as dessert in Sardinian restaurants.

name: Malloreddus alla Campidanese
description: Small ridged durum wheat gnocchetti traditionally flavoured with saffron, served 'alla campidanese' with a sausage and tomato sauce and pecorino. A typical Sardinian pasta, cooked for festivals and weddings.
how_to_order: Ask for 'malloreddus alla campidanese'.

name: Mirto
description: Sweet liqueur made by macerating myrtle berries in alcohol; the red version uses dark berries, the white uses pale berries or, less often, young leaves. 'Mirto di Sardegna' is the name adopted by the Sardinian region and producers.
how_to_eat: Sip chilled after a meal.
how_to_order: Ask for a 'mirto' as a digestivo.
